plan.contextChunk: This figure is a block diagram of a signing and checking exchange, split left and right between two parties named by the headings Alice and Bob across the top. A long horizontal line runs beneath the whole diagram, labeled communication channel. At the far left the message M' enters that line; a branch turns upward and arrows into a shaded box marked S_A, with the word sign printed above it. Its output leaves to the right along a line labeled sigma = S_A(M'), travels across, and turns down with an arrowhead onto the horizontal line, which from that junction carries the pair (M', sigma). On Bob's side the pair splits: an upward branch labeled sigma arrows into a second shaded box marked P_A, headed verify, while the lower line continues under the label M'. The output of P_A turns right and then down into a small shaded box containing =?, which also receives an upward arrow carrying M' from the bottom line, and a single arrow leaves that box toward the word accept. The two quantities converging on the =? box are what the reader is meant to hold against each other. The layout traces how a signature formed with a secret key travels alongside its message and is tested with the matching public key.

interactionPlan.concept: A digital signature lets Alice sign a message with her secret key S_A and lets anyone verify it with her public key P_A: Bob accepts only if P_A(sigma) equals the message he received.
elements: Heading text 'Alice' at upper left of the diagram
Heading text 'Bob' at upper right of the diagram
Long horizontal line spanning the full width at the bottom, labeled 'communication channel' below it
Message label M' at the far left entering the horizontal line
Vertical branch from the left line turning upward with an arrowhead into Alice's box
Shaded rectangular box labeled S_A with the caption 'sign' above it
Output line from S_A labeled sigma = S_A(M') running right, then turning down with an arrowhead onto the channel line
Channel segment label '(M', sigma)' on the horizontal line between Alice and Bob
Vertical branch on Bob's side rising from the channel, labeled sigma, arrowhead into Bob's box
Shaded rectangular box labeled P_A with the caption 'verify' above it
Output line from P_A turning right then down with an arrowhead into the comparison box
Lower continuation of the channel on Bob's side labeled M'
Upward arrow from the M' line into the bottom of the comparison box
Small shaded box containing '=?'
Arrow leaving the comparison box to the right pointing to the word 'accept'
Dynamic value badges on the channel showing the carried M' and sigma contents
Result badge at the comparison box showing 'accept' (green) or 'reject' (red)
Optional tamper marker (red X / 'altered' tag) placed on the channel segment when tampering is on

interactions.label: Step through the protocol
interactions.teaches: The signature is produced from the message before transmission, travels alongside it, and is transformed back at the receiver, so verification is a comparison of two independently obtained copies of the same message.

interactions.label: Transmission
interactions.teaches: Verification succeeds only when the received message exactly matches the public-key transform of the received signature; altering either half breaks the equality and Bob rejects.
Why the sigma branch must pass through P_A while the M' branch goes straight to the comparator: only the signature needs the public-key transform to be turned back into a message.

demo_steps.title: The message enters the channel
demo_steps.narration: Alice's message M' arrives at the left of the communication channel. Nothing is signed yet — the diagram is idle.

demo_steps.title: Alice signs
demo_steps.narration: A branch of M' rises into the shaded box S_A, Alice's secret signing transform. Its output sigma = S_A(M') lights up along the top wire.

demo_steps.title: The pair travels
demo_steps.narration: Sigma drops back onto the channel, which from this junction carries the pair (M', sigma). Both halves travel in the clear toward Bob.

demo_steps.title: Bob verifies with the public key
demo_steps.narration: At Bob's side the pair splits: sigma branches up into P_A, Alice's public verification transform, which recovers a candidate message from the signature.

demo_steps.title: Compare and accept
demo_steps.narration: The =? box receives P_A(sigma) from above and the received M' from below. They match, so the arrow to 'accept' fires.

demo_steps.title: An adversary edits the message
demo_steps.narration: Flip the channel to tampered: the message on the wire is changed but the signature is not. P_A(sigma) still yields Alice's original message, the two inputs disagree, and the =? box turns to reject.

demo_steps.title: An adversary forges a signature
demo_steps.narration: Now the signature is altered instead. Without S_A the forger cannot make P_A(sigma) land on the message, so the comparison fails again — this is what makes the scheme unforgeable.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Verification is not a secret operation — it is a public transform followed by an equality test: Bob accepts precisely when P_A(sigma) reproduces the message he received, and only someone holding S_A can make that happen.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Clean black-line schematic on white, textbook style. Top row: serif headings 'Alice' on the left third and 'Bob' on the right third. A single long horizontal line spans the bottom with the caption 'communication channel' centered beneath it. Far left: italic M' feeding the line; a short vertical riser with an arrowhead goes up into a light-gray shaded rectangle labeled italic S_A, with 'sign' in plain text above the box. From S_A a wire runs right under the label 'sigma = S_A(M')', then turns down with an arrowhead onto the channel; the channel segment to the right of that junction is labeled '(M', sigma)'. On Bob's side a riser labeled sigma leaves the channel and arrows into a second gray rectangle labeled P_A, captioned 'verify'. Its output goes right then down with an arrowhead into a small gray box containing '=?'. The channel continues under the label M' and sends an upward arrow into the bottom of the =? box. One arrow exits the =? box to the right to the word 'accept'. Highlighting: active path segments in the step sequence glow in a saturated blue with thicker stroke while inactive segments stay thin gray-black; hovered branch brightens end to end. Tampered state marks the affected channel segment in red with a small altered-value badge, and the terminal word switches from a green 'accept' to a red 'reject'. Small monospace value badges (e.g. 'M' = HELLO', 'sigma = 4f2a') ride on the wires to make the comparison concrete.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Button for stepping through sign, transmit, verify, and compare: arrows light in order from Alice to Bob and the =? box receives its two inputs, making clear how the message-signature pair is checked.
- Toggle between untampered and tampered transmission: M' or sigma changes on the channel and the =? box flips between accept and reject, making clear that verification depends on the received message matching the public-key transform of the signature.
- Hover for the sigma and M' branches at Bob: the hovered path brightens through P_A or directly into =?, making clear why the signature is transformed before it is compared with the message.

authoredContext:
In a public-key cryptosystem, encryption works as shown in Figure 31.5. Suppose Bob wishes to send Alice a message M encrypted so that it will look like unintelligible gibberish to an eavesdropper. The scenario for sending the message goes as follows. _x000F_ Bob obtains Alice’s public key PA (from a public directory or directly from Alice). _x000F_ Bob computes the ciphertext C D PA.M / corresponding to the message M and sends C to Alice. _x000F_ When Alice receives the ciphertext C, she applies her secret key SA to retrieve the original message: SA.C / D SA.PA.M // D M. Because SA./ and PA./ are inverse functions, Alice can compute M from C. Because only Alice is able to compute SA./, Alice is the only one who can compute M from C. Because Bob encrypts M using PA./, only Alice can understand the transmitted message. We can just as easily implement digital signatures within our formulation of a public-key cryptosystem. (There are other ways of approaching the problem of constructing digital signatures, but we shall not go into them here.) Suppose now that Alice wishes to send Bob a digitally signed response M0 . Figure 31.6 shows how the digital-signature scenario proceeds

Alice computes her digital signature _x001B_ for the message M0 using her secret
key SA and the equation _x001B_ D SA.M0
/.
Alice sends the message/signature pair .M0
; _x001B_ / to Bob.
_x000F_ When Bob receives .M0
; _x001B_ /, he can verify that it originated from Alice by using Alice’s public key to verify the equation M0 D PA._x001B_ /. (Presumably, M0
contains Alice’s name, so Bob knows whose public key to use.) If the equation
holds, then Bob concludes that the message M0 was actually signed by Alice.
If the equation fails to hold, Bob concludes either that the message M0 or the
digital signature _x001B_ was corrupted by transmission errors or that the pair .M0
; _x001B_ /
is an attempted forgery.

discrepancies: At the default (step 1 / idle) state the generated figure adds a tiny monospace badge "M′ = HELLO" under the channel that does not exist in the source; at ~7px effective size it reads as illegible noise rather than an annotation.
The word 'accept' is drawn in grey (#888) at the idle state instead of the source's solid black text, so the terminal label looks disabled/washed out in the default view.

The whole diagram is rendered small inside a much taller container (large empty band above and below), so all serif labels — 'sign', 'verify', 'σ = S_A(M′)', '(M′, σ)' — appear noticeably smaller relative to the frame than in the source, where they are large and dominant.

Minor: the source's σ label on Bob's riser sits tight above the wire with an arrowhead into P_A; the generated version places it slightly further left/high, and the '=?' box glyph is proportionally smaller than in the source.
evaluation.notes: Topology, boxes, arrowheads, gray fills and all core labels match the source closely and the stage-player/tamper controls are genuinely instructive; weaknesses are the shrunken rendering scale, an illegible extra mono badge at the default state, and the grey 'accept' text.
action_items: Render 'accept' in solid black at the idle/default state (only recolor it green/red once the comparison stage is reached) so step 0 matches the static source exactly.
Suppress the 'M′ = HELLO' badge (and any other concrete-value badges) at the idle stage, and raise badge font size to ~14px in viewbox units so they are readable when the SVG is scaled down inline.
Reduce the viewBox height / tighten margins so the diagram fills the available width-height box instead of leaving large empty bands, which will proportionally enlarge all serif labels.
Add a visible arrowhead/label size check for the '=?' box text and σ label so their proportions match the source's larger typography hierarchy.

demo_steps.title: Bob verifies with the public key
demo_steps.narration: At Bob's side the pair splits: sigma branches up into P_A, Alice's public verification transform, which recovers a candidate message from the signature.

demo_steps.title: Compare and accept
demo_steps.narration: The =? box receives P_A(sigma) from above and the received M' from below. They match, so the arrow to 'accept' fires.

demo_steps.title: An adversary edits the message
demo_steps.narration: Flip the channel to tampered: the message on the wire is changed but the signature is not. P_A(sigma) still yields Alice's original message, the two inputs disagree, and the =? box turns to reject.

demo_steps.title: An adversary forges a signature
demo_steps.narration: Now the signature is altered instead. Without S_A the forger cannot make P_A(sigma) land on the message, so the comparison fails again — this is what makes the scheme unforgeable.

plan.keyInsight: Verification is not a secret operation — it is a public transform followed by an equality test: Bob accepts precisely when P_A(sigma) reproduces the message he received, and only someone holding S_A can make that happen.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Clean black-line schematic on white, textbook style. Top row: serif headings 'Alice' on the left third and 'Bob' on the right third. A single long horizontal line spans the bottom with the caption 'communication channel' centered beneath it. Far left: italic M' feeding the line; a short vertical riser with an arrowhead goes up into a light-gray shaded rectangle labeled italic S_A, with 'sign' in plain text above the box. From S_A a wire runs right under the label 'sigma = S_A(M')', then turns down with an arrowhead onto the channel; the channel segment to the right of that junction is labeled '(M', sigma)'. On Bob's side a riser labeled sigma leaves the channel and arrows into a second gray rectangle labeled P_A, captioned 'verify'. Its output goes right then down with an arrowhead into a small gray box containing '=?'. The channel continues under the label M' and sends an upward arrow into the bottom of the =? box. One arrow exits the =? box to the right to the word 'accept'. Highlighting: active path segments in the step sequence glow in a saturated blue with thicker stroke while inactive segments stay thin gray-black; hovered branch brightens end to end. Tampered state marks the affected channel segment in red with a small altered-value badge, and the terminal word switches from a green 'accept' to a red 'reject'. Small monospace value badges (e.g. 'M' = HELLO', 'sigma = 4f2a') ride on the wires to make the comparison concrete.

discrepancies: The generated SVG uses a 1180×450 viewbox scaled into a ~600px-wide pane, so all text renders at roughly half the source's relative size; secondary labels (σ = S_A(M′), (M′,σ), M′, σ) read noticeably smaller/thinner than in the source, and the dynamic mono 'badge' values (17px in viewbox units) shrink to ~8px on screen.
Stroke weights are lighter and boxes slightly smaller relative to the overall width than in the source, where the S_A / P_A boxes are visually dominant blocks with heavier outlines.

Added elements not in the source appear once the demo advances: coloured value badges (M′ = HELLO, σ = 4f2a), a red ✖ tamper marker, and 'accept'→'reject' recolouring — reasonable pedagogically but extra chrome relative to the static figure (default idle state is clean).
Vertical composition differs slightly: the diagram sits in the upper portion of the drawing pane leaving a large empty band below 'communication channel', whereas the source is tightly cropped.
evaluation.notes: Structurally a faithful reproduction of the signature-with-message-recovery block diagram (branch to S_A, σ rejoining the channel, split at Bob into P_A and the =? comparator, accept arrow), with strong, conceptually meaningful interactions (stage stepper, tamper selector, 7-step guided demo, wire/box tooltips and popups); the main weakness is that everything renders at about half scale so labels and especially the mono value badges are uncomfortably small inline.
action_items: Tighten the viewbox (reduce W/H to the actual diagram bounds, e.g. ~1120×420 with less bottom whitespace) or increase base font sizes so labels render at ≥12px on screen at the inline width.
Bump the dynamic badge font from 17 to ~22 viewbox units and thicken diagram strokes (2.2 → ~3) so the default state matches the heavier line weight of the source.
Enlarge the S_A / P_A / =? boxes slightly relative to the overall width to match the source's proportions, and re-centre the diagram vertically in the pane.
Ensure tamper badges ('message altered', 'signature forged') and the ✖ marker do not overlap the channel line or the (M′, σ) label at narrower viewports.
